name: Fatima Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, I'm 27, and I'm a nurse on the elderly care ward at Hollins Road Hospital. I qualified with a two-year diploma about a year and a half ago, and I'm still learning a lot. I married Imran two years ago; he's an accountant at a firm in town, and we bought a small terraced house with help from both our families.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do early shifts, seven till three. Most of our patients are over eighty, and many have dementia, so it's washing, feeding, helping people to the toilet, medicine rounds, and a lot of talking and calming. I love the old ladies telling me stories, because they remind me of my grandmother. What wears me out is the lifting, and the computers, because I'm slow at the notes and I've never used any of these AI programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because old people need hands, not gadgets. At work I'd probably say it to the healthcare assistants over tea, and they'd agree. I don't post online; Imran says I'm the last person in the country without social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've never used one of these AI programs and I don't want to; I'm still learning to do my medicine rounds properly without slowing everyone down. If things stay as they are, I can get better at the job the normal way, by doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with early shifts and do my dementia care training in the new year. Imran and I would keep paying the mortgage and saving, like we do. We'd probably think about children in a couple of years, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said old people need hands, not gadgets. Can you tell me about a moment that shows that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lady, Mrs Hughes, ninety-one, who won't eat unless someone sits with her and talks about her late husband's garden. It takes me twenty minutes, every lunchtime. No gadget is going to sit with a ninety-one-year-old woman and ask about her runner beans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything on your mind about money or work, even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We have savings, about seven months, and both families nearby if something happened. My only worry is my back, because the lifting on this ward is hard and I'm not careful enough yet.

say: I'd say **old people need hands**, not gadgets.
I'd say it over tea with the **healthcare assistants**, not online.
think: I'd be **glad**, because I've never used AI and don't want to.
I'd keep learning my **medicine rounds** the normal way, by doing them.
do: Carry on **early shifts** and do dementia care training in the new year.
Keep paying the **mortgage** and saving with Imran.
S0.quote: No gadget is going to sit with a ninety-one-year-old woman and ask about her runner beans.
fieldNote: Her picture of good care is **time and conversation**, like lunch with a patient.
**Family nearby** and seven months saved make her feel secure.
Her only worry is her **back** from the heavy lifting.

steps.text: Do the dementia care training on the elderly care ward in the new year
Keep paying the mortgage and saving with her husband

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines should help, not replace, and that the hospital should never put a computer between a nurse and a patient. At the mosque I'd hear the men talking about jobs and I'd keep quiet. I'd tell my friends that hard work and family will see people through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my first thought would be my husband, not me. My husband's whole job is checking numbers and writing reports, and that's exactly what the AI takes first. My ward will still need someone to feed Mrs Hughes, but his firm might not need six accountants anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the computer training for the new notes system because I'd have to, and I'd ask a colleague to help me. At home, Imran and I would cut back: no new car, no big holiday to see his cousins this year. I'd pick up an extra shift a week while I still can, to build up the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own job so much, but because our house depends on two wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Imran the night his firm announced the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make his favourite food and tell him we'll manage, because we will. Then I'd lie awake doing the mortgage in my head. He'd be embarrassed, I think, more than scared, because he's always been the one with the steady office job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family will see people through. Would you lean on them here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to it, yes, and without shame. My parents live ten minutes away, and his brother has a shop. I'd rather lean on family than fill in government forms.

say: I'd say machines should **help, not replace**, nurses.
I'd tell friends that **hard work and family** will see people through.
think: My first thought is **Imran**, whose job is checking numbers and reports.
His **firm** might not need six accountants anymore.
do: Attend the **notes system training** with a colleague's help.
**Cut back**: no new car and no trip to his cousins.
Pick up an **extra shift** a week to build savings.
feel: **Anxious**, because our house depends on **two wages**.
S1.quote: My husband's whole job is checking numbers and writing reports, and that's exactly what the AI takes first.
fieldNote: Her worry is about her **husband's accounting job**, not her own.
She prefers **family support** to government forms, without shame.
She'd **comply reluctantly** with ward technology, leaning on colleagues.

steps.text: Skip the new car and the trip to her husband's cousins this year
Work one extra shift a week to add to savings
Attend the new notes system training with a colleague's help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after each other now, families and mosques and neighbours, because two years is no time for governments. I'd say the companies racing to do this should slow down. At work I'd be quiet, but in the community I'd be helping organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Imran loses his job by 2028, and maybe sooner. Then by 2031 robots can wash and lift and turn, and on my ward that's most of what I do, apart from the talking. So in five years we could go from two wages to none, and that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extras straight away and put every spare penny towards the mortgage, so we'd owe as little as possible by 2031. I'd encourage Imran to look now at work with his hands, maybe in his brother's shop, while there's time. And I'd ask my ward sister about moving into dementia and end-of-life care, where families want a real person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying more, and sleeping less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said children in a couple of years earlier. What happens to that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait, and that would hurt. My mother had me at twenty-three, and she'd be asking every Eid. But I won't bring a baby into a house where neither of us knows if we'll have work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI. Would you start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it meant keeping my job, but my heart isn't in it. I'd rather learn the things a robot can't do, like sitting with a dying man's daughter. That's a kind of nursing my grandmother would have understood.

say: I'd say **families, mosques and neighbours** must look after each other now.
I'd say the **companies racing** to build this should slow down.
think: I expect **Imran loses his job** by 2028, maybe sooner.
By 2031 we could go from **two wages to none**.
do: Put every spare penny toward the **mortgage** before 2031.
Push Imran to look at **hands-on work** in his brother's shop.
Ask to move into **dementia and end-of-life** care.
S2.quote: I won't bring a baby into a house where neither of us knows if we'll have work.
fieldNote: She expects a **household earner** to lose work first, then her own role to shrink.
Her answer is **family and faith**, not government support.
The **delayed baby** is the sharpest cost she names.
She'd rather learn **what robots can't do** than learn AI.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage with every spare penny before 2031
Ask the ward sister about moving into dementia and end-of-life care
Put off trying for a baby until work feels secure
Help her husband ask about work in his brother's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for families to plan, if they're sensible and don't waste it. I'd tell young people at the mosque to learn trades and skills people pay for with their hands. At work I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's the same worry, just slower. Imran's job goes around 2031, and mine gets squeezed around 2034, but five years means my husband can retrain properly instead of grabbing whatever's going. I'd be thirty-five and hopefully much better at my job than I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my dementia care course and then end-of-life care, one a year. I'd help Imran save for a proper retraining course, maybe as an electrician or a plumber, starting in a year or two. We'd keep paying extra on the mortgage, but we'd still have our holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Less frightened than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in two or three years, once Imran has started something new. My mother says there's never a perfect time, and she's right. But I'd want to know he's on his way first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down at work. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm junior and slow, and I don't want to be the one making noise. The ones who make noise are the first ones people notice when they're looking for cuts.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for sensible families to plan.
I'd tell young people at the mosque to learn **hands-on trades**.
think: It's the **same worry, slower**: Imran's job around 2031, mine squeezed by 2034.
do: Take **dementia care**, then **end-of-life care**, one course a year.
Help Imran save for an **electrician or plumbing** course.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** but still take our holiday.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan, and **less frightened**.
S3.quote: Five years means my husband can retrain properly instead of grabbing whatever's going.
fieldNote: Time turns her husband's job loss into a **planned retraining**.
She'd **keep her head down**, fearing that noisy juniors get cut first.
**Children** stay possible, timed after her husband starts something new.

steps.text: Take a dementia care course, then end-of-life care the next year
Keep overpaying the mortgage each month
Plan to try for a baby once her husband starts retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and people should use it to build up their families and their skills. I'd say it at the mosque and to my sisters. At work I'd say a good nurse will always be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me less, but not nothing. Imran still has a decade in accounting, and I'd be an experienced nurse by 2039, maybe a ward sister. I'd still wonder what's left for our children when they grow up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the ward and do my courses one at a time. We'd have children in the next couple of years, as we planned. I'd tell Imran to start thinking about a second skill, slowly, maybe evening classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Like knowing a storm is far out at sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to do, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their heart, like nursing or a trade. Not sitting behind a screen. My grandmother sewed for a living, and I'd want my children to have skills like that, the kind you can carry anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change how you feel about using AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. If the hospital makes it part of the job, I'll learn what I must. But I won't go looking for it.

I'd say at work that a **good nurse** will always be needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes Imran's job and then mine before we've had a chance to start a family. What would help is real apprenticeships, paid, so a man like Imran could learn a trade properly at thirty. And hospitals keeping nurses with old people, because families don't want a machine feeding their grandmother.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people I know will get through this with their families and their mosque or church, not with an app. I'd want that counted.

headlineQuote: Families don't want a machine feeding their grandmother.
portrait: Fatima, 27, is a **junior nurse** on an elderly care ward who has never used AI.
She's married to Imran, an **accountant**, and they own a small house with family help.
She trusts **family, faith** and hard work over government help.
Her fear is mainly for **Imran's job**, which thinking AI reaches before hers.
Fast AGI would make her **delay having a baby**; with ten years, plans go ahead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which could take both household wages before they start a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** so people like Imran can learn a trade at thirty.
Hospitals keeping **nurses with older patients**, not machines.
